name: INA181A2IDBVR
title: INA181, INA2181, INA4181: bidirectional voltage-output current-sense amplifiers, –0.2 V to 26 V common mode, gains 20 to 200 V/V
summary: Single, dual and quad current-sense amplifiers that measure the drop across a shunt at a common-mode voltage from –0.2 V to 26 V, on the high side or the low side, regardless of their 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply. Each channel has a fixed gain of 20, 50, 100 or 200 V/V (A1 to A4) from a matched internal resistor network, and a REF pin that offsets the output for bidirectional measurement. INA181 comes in SOT-23-6 and SC70-6, INA2181 in VSSOP-10 and WSON-10, INA4181 in TSSOP-20; all are specified from –40 °C to 125 °C. INA181A2IDBVR is the single-channel, gain-50 part in SOT-23-6.
key_figures: ±150 µV max at VIN+ = 0 V; ±500 µV max at 12 V

circuits.title: Unidirectional application
circuits.description: High-side sensing with REF tied to ground: the output sits at ground with no current and rises as current flows from the bus through the shunt to the load. CBYPASS decouples VS.

parts.value: power supply VS, 2.7 V to 5.5 V

circuits.title: Measuring bidirectional current
circuits.description: High-side sensing with REF set by a reference voltage, so the output rests at VREF and moves above it for current toward the load and below it for current the other way. A selector connects REF either to the reference voltage directly (S1) or to a buffer amplifier (S2) that follows the midpoint of a divider R1, R2 across the reference voltage. In the design example VS is 5 V, the bus 12 V, the shunt 1 mΩ, the part an INA181A3 and VREF 2.5 V for ±20 A.

parts.value: power supply VS, 2.7 V to 5.5 V

notes: S1 and S2 are the two positions of one single-pole, double-throw switch.

circuits.title: Switching the supply off, REF grounded
circuits.description: A P-channel MOSFET between the supply and VS turns the amplifier on and off. RPULL-UP holds the gate at the supply so the switch is off until the Shutdown line pulls the gate low. CBYPASS sits on the switched VS node; REF is grounded.

circuits.title: Basic connections
circuits.description: High-side sensing into a microcontroller ADC. OUT drives the ADC input; REF returns to ground by way of the ADC reference so both share one ground point. An RC filter between OUT and the ADC gives the best performance. CBYPASS decouples VS.

parts.value: power supply VS, 2.7 V to 5.5 V

circuits.title: Filter at the input pins
circuits.description: Two series resistors under 10 Ω and a capacitor across the inputs form a differential low-pass ahead of IN+ and IN–, with f–3dB = 1 / (2π (RF + RF) CF). The series resistors add gain error set by the internal input resistance.

circuits.title: Summing two currents
circuits.description: Both channels of an INA2181 sense loads fed from one supply through equal shunts. OUT1 drives REF2, so OUT2 = (ILOAD1 + ILOAD2) × RSENSE × GAIN; REF1 is grounded and sets the zero point of the sum.

circuits.title: Detecting leakage currents
circuits.description: One INA2181 channel senses the current into a load, the other the current out of it with its inputs swapped. OUT1 drives REF2, so the two readings subtract and OUT2 stays at VREF1 when the currents match; any leakage moves OUT2 away from VREF1 in either direction.

circuits.title: Transient protection with two Zener diodes
circuits.description: For common-mode transients beyond 26 V each input gets a series resistor of 10 Ω or less and a Zener diode from the input pin to ground, so the Zener clamps the pin while the resistor limits its current. REF is grounded; CBYPASS decouples VS.

circuits.title: Transient protection with one transorb and input clamps
circuits.description: Where small Zeners cannot absorb the energy, one transorb from IN– to ground takes the transient and a back-to-back pair of diodes across IN+ and IN– limits the differential voltage. Each input has a series resistor under 10 Ω. REF is grounded; CBYPASS decouples VS.

operation.text: Each channel is a difference amplifier: matched internal resistors around an op amp set the fixed gain, IN+ and IN– enter through input resistors, and the non-inverting side is referred to REF. The input common-mode range, –0.2 V to 26 V, does not depend on VS while VS is between 2.7 V and 5.5 V, so the same part works on the high side or the low side of a load.

Small-signal bandwidth reaches 350 kHz (A1) and slew rate is 2 V/µs. Uses named for this speed are low-side motor current control and fast out-of-range detection with an external comparator and reference.
A voltage on REF offsets the output. Positive sense voltage (IN+ above IN–) drives the output above VREF; negative sense voltage drives it below.

At VCM = 0 V the offset is within ±150 µV, which allows a smaller shunt and less loss and keeps accuracy at the low end of the current range. Gain error is within 1 %; at large sense voltages it dominates the error.

Specified swing is within 30 mV of VS and 5 mV of GND, measured with the input overdriven. With VREF = 0 V, a positive offset times gain can hold the zero-current output above the swing limit: an INA181A4 with +40 µV offset sits at 8 mV; with –40 µV the swing limit applies. Offset grows with common-mode voltage through CMRR, raising the zero-current output at high VCM.

The output equals the IN+ to IN– difference times gain plus VREF when VS is 2.7 V to 5.5 V, VCM is –0.2 V to 26 V, the largest signal times gain plus VREF stays below VS less the positive swing, and the smallest signal times gain plus VREF stays above the swing to GND.

REF tied to ground puts the output at ground for zero current; current from bus to load raises the output. To measure very small currents, bias REF above 50 mV so the output is in its linear range, and drive REF from a buffer to avoid common-mode rejection error. REF may instead go to VS: the output then rests about 200 mV below VS and moves down only for negative sense voltage. REF must not exceed VS.
REF may be set anywhere from 0 V to VS; mid-supply gives equal range in both directions, and an off-centre value suits unequal currents. Battery charge/discharge and motor drives are typical uses.

If the sense voltage times gain exceeds the swing range the output goes as near the rail or ground as it can and does not track the input. After a fault overload ends the output recovers in about 20 µs. Driving the output into a rail does not harm the part within the absolute maximum ratings, and the output keeps its polarity with no phase reversal. If overload happens in normal use, use a smaller shunt or a lower-gain option.

There is no shutdown pin; VS can be switched by a logic gate or transistor. Unpowered, each input still sees typically more than 500 kΩ to OUT and to REF, so input current depends on the voltages there; a disabled output stage is a low-impedance path to ground. With VS powered and the shunt common-mode voltage above VS, each input draws an additional, well-matched 55 µA typical; below VS that current is negligible.
IN+ and IN– withstand the full 26 V differential input range whether or not VS is applied. The output range is bounded by VS.
VS needs a bypass capacitor of at least 0.1 µF placed close to the VS and GND pins; noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more decoupling.

A larger shunt raises the signal and shrinks the offset's share of the error, but the inputs draw typically 75 µA each at 12 V common mode, so shunts above a few ohms add offset error and degrade CMRR. The shunt's power budget sets a ceiling (RSENSE < PDMAX / IMAX²), the positive swing limit caps RSENSE × GAIN, and the negative swing limit sets a floor; raising VREF slightly also helps against the negative limit.

With a high-impedance load the best place for a filter is an RC from OUT to GND, which also attenuates disturbances on the common-mode voltage and supply. An input filter uses series resistors of 10 Ω or less: the internal bias network makes the input bias currents unequal when a differential voltage is present, and that mismatch across the resistors appears as a gain error given by the gain error factor equations.
Tying OUT of one channel to REF of the next adds the channels: the last output is (ILOAD1 + ILOAD2) × RSENSE × GAIN plus the first channel's VREF. All shunts must have the same value.

The same chain with the second channel's inputs reversed subtracts the currents into and out of a load; with equal shunts OUT2 equals VREF1 when they match. A reference on REF1 keeps the output off ground so a difference of either sign shows.

For VS = 5 V, VCM = 12 V, ±20 A, under 450 mW in the shunt: RSENSE ≤ 1.125 mΩ, so 1 mΩ. With VREF = 2.5 V the positive swing allows a gain up to 122.5 and the negative swing up to 124.75, so the gain-100 INA181A3. Offset of 500 µV maximum at 20 A is 2.5 %; with 1 % gain error the root-sum-square total is 2.7 %, inside 3.5 %. The A3 bandwidth, 150 kHz, meets the 100 kHz need.

Common-mode transients beyond 26 V call for Zener diodes or Zener-type transient absorbers only; other absorbers respond too slowly. Series resistors of about 10 Ω give the Zeners a working impedance; larger values add gain error. Low-power Zeners in SOT-523 or SOD-523 suffice for short transients; for more energy, one transorb plus back-to-back diodes across the inputs. Either way the board area is under an SO-8 footprint.

Use a Kelvin (4-wire) connection from the shunt to IN+ and IN–, keep the two traces matched in length, and put the 0.1 µF bypass capacitor as near VS and GND as possible. REF goes to a low-impedance reference or to GND when unused.
AEC-Q100 qualified versions are INA181-Q1, INA2181-Q1 and INA4181-Q1.
